identity.title: SNAT2-mediated amino acid import maintains osmotic balance to restrain macrophage metabolic reprogramming and inflammasome activation.

content.abstract: Macrophages undergo metabolic reprogramming during inflammatory responses to microbial infection, in part because of activation of the transcription factor HIF-1alpha (hypoxia-inducible factor 1alpha). Here, we identified regulators of HIF-1alpha-dependent gene expression during immune activation induced by lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and during the hypoxic response using genome-wide CRISPR screens in cultured mouse macrophages. The small neutral amino acid transporter SNAT2 (encoded by Slc38a2) was a key inhibitor of HIF-1alpha activation and metabolic reprogramming in cultured and bone marrow-derived mouse macrophages in response to LPS but not to hypoxia. Inflammatory stimulation increased SNAT2 protein abundance and dynamically expanded intracellular amino acid pools in a largely SNAT2-dependent manner. Consistent with the role of intracellular amino acids as osmolytes, SNAT2 deficiency resulted in osmotic imbalance and aberrant activation of NFAT5, a central transcriptional regulator of osmotic stress responses. In turn, NFAT5 promoted nitric oxide- and HIF-1alpha-dependent metabolic reprogramming and augmented NLRP3 inflammasome activation under hyperosmotic conditions. Supplementation with organic osmolytes mitigated both the excessive metabolic reprogramming and hyperosmotic inflammasome activation in SNAT2-deficient macrophages. Consistent with the heightened inflammatory phenotype in vitro, myeloid-specific deletion of SNAT2 reduced bacterial burden in mice infected with Listeria monocytogenes. Together, these findings identify SNAT2 as a negative feedback regulator that restrains macrophage metabolic reprogramming and inflammatory activation by maintaining amino acid availability that supports osmotic homeostasis.
